figures.name: Apprenticeship Levy allowance

tokens: The amount of the levy allowance is £15,000

sources.citation: Finance Act 2016, c. 24 s. 99(5) ("The amount of the levy allowance is £15,000 (except where section 101 or 102 provides otherwise)")
https://www.gov.uk/guidance/rates-and-thresholds-for-employers-2026-to-2027 ("Apprenticeship Levy allowance £15,000")

definitions.text: The Apprenticeship Levy allowance: the annual amount an employer may offset against its Apprenticeship Levy charge, so that the levy bites only on a pay bill above £3 million at the 0.5% charge.

applicability.note: An annual allowance for the tax year, applied against the levy charge as it accrues through the year.
applicability.article: Finance Act 2016 s.99(1)-(5)

figures.scope_note: s.99(5) itself defers to ss.101 and 102: connected companies form a company unit and must DIVIDE one £15,000 allowance between them, and s.102 does the same for connected charities. This figure is the allowance itself, never a member's share of it.
figures.notes: The first sweep targeted s.101, following the checklist's "Finance Act 2016 Pt 6", and refused: s.101 states £15,000 five times as a total to be divided between company-unit members, so the tokens matched several sibling provisions. s.99(5) is the provision that sets the amount. effective_from is the Act's Royal Assent, read from the archived section's own ukm:EnactmentDate ("2016-09-15") and matched by the RestrictStartDate on the P1group holding s.99. The archived s.99 states no first-charged tax year — it charges the levy "for a tax year" without naming one — and s.98 is not archived, so 6 April of the first charging year is not a date this record can read from bytes. GOV.UK's "2017-18" is guidance, not the section, and stays in the scope note.

sources.citation: Finance Act 2016, c. 24 s. 99(6) ("For the purposes of this section the 'relevant percentage' is 0.5%"), applied by s. 99(1)-(2) to the employer's pay bill for the tax year less the levy allowance
https://www.gov.uk/api/content/guidance/pay-apprenticeship-levy ("Apprenticeship Levy is charged at 0.5% of your annual pay bill")

definitions.text: The rate of the Apprenticeship Levy: the percentage of an employer's annual pay bill charged as levy, before the levy allowance is set against it (Finance Act 2016 s.99).

applicability.note: Charged on the pay bill for the tax year; paid monthly through PAYE on the cumulative pay bill, with the allowance spread across the year.
applicability.article: Finance Act 2016 s.99(1)-(2)

figures.scope_note: The £15,000 allowance in s.99(5) is `apprenticeship_levy.allowance`; connected companies and charities share one allowance under s.101-102. Neither the rate nor the allowance has moved since the levy began in the 2017-18 tax year.

figures.name: Employment Allowance (maximum)

sources.citation: National Insurance Contributions Act 2014, c. 7 s. 1(2)(a) ("The person's employment allowance for the tax year is — (a) £10,500 or (b) if less, an amount equal to the total amount of the liabilities mentioned in subsection (1)(b) which are not excluded liabilities")
https://www.gov.uk/guidance/rates-and-thresholds-for-employers-2026-to-2027 ("Employment Allowance for 2026 to 2027 is £10,500")

definitions.text: The maximum Employment Allowance: the largest amount an eligible employer may set against its secondary Class 1 National Insurance liability for the tax year. It is a CEILING, not a payment — s.1(2) allows the lesser of this amount and the employer's own qualifying secondary liabilities, so an employer whose liability is smaller claims only that smaller amount.

applicability.note: Claimed against secondary Class 1 liabilities of the tax year; the allowance is annual and is set against liability as it arises through the year.
applicability.article: National Insurance Contributions Act 2014 s.1(1)-(2)

figures.scope_note: The £100,000 secondary-liability eligibility cap was removed from 6 April 2025, so the allowance is no longer restricted by the size of the previous year's bill. Excluded liabilities (s.2) and single-director companies remain out of scope.
figures.notes: An act carry: NICA 2014 s.1(2)(a) states the cash figure itself, and the probe finds no textual amendment touching it after the value took effect. Successive increases (£2,000 as enacted, then £3,000, £4,000, £5,000, £10,500) were made by amending this provision, so the current text is the figure. effective_from is the date the last of those amendments put £10,500 there, read from the F-note on the archived section: "Sum in s. 1(2)(a) substituted (6.4.2025) by National Insurance Contributions (Secondary Class 1 Contributions) Act 2025 (c. 11), s. 3(2)(4)" — provenance by an Act, on the value's own start date.

figures.name: Additional adoption leave: weeks

tokens: additional adoption leave period is a period of 26 weeks beginning on the day after

sources.citation: https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2002/2788/made (SI 2002/2788 reg 20(2) as made: "Subject to regulations 22 and 24, an employee's additional adoption leave period is a period of 26 weeks beginning on the day after the last day of his ordinary adoption leave period"; in force 8 December 2002, reg 1, applying to children matched or placed on or after 6 April 2003, reg 3(2))
https://www.gov.uk/adoption-pay-leave (under "Leave": "Statutory Adoption Leave is 52 weeks. It's made up of: 26 weeks of Ordinary Adoption Leave 26 weeks of Additional Adoption Leave")

definitions.text: The additional adoption leave period: a further 26 weeks beginning the day after ordinary adoption leave ends (regulation 20(2) of the Paternity and Adoption Leave Regulations 2002). It runs on from the ordinary period without a gap, which is why the two together are a year.
definitions.instrument: Paternity and Adoption Leave Regulations 2002 reg 20(2)

applicability.note: Begins the day after the ordinary adoption leave period ends (reg 20(2)), so it attaches to the placement through that period rather than to a tax year. Regulation 20(1) confines it to an employee who took ordinary adoption leave and whose placement has not ended. Regulations 22 and 24 can end it early. Dated 6 April 2003 on regulation 3(2), as the ordinary period is.
applicability.article: Paternity and Adoption Leave Regulations 2002 regs 1, 3(2), 20(1), 20(2), 22, 24

figures.scope_note: 26 weeks on top of the ordinary 26, and unpaid for most of its length: Statutory Adoption Pay runs 39 weeks from the start of the ordinary period, so the last 13 weeks of this one carry no statutory pay. The ordinary limb is `employment.leave.adoption.ordinary_weeks` and the 52-week total is the derived companion `employment.leave.adoption_weeks`.
figures.notes: An SI carry (ADR-0014), and a HOST-STATES one: no textual amendment touches regulation 20(2). The locator runs on past the number to "beginning on the day after", because regulation 18(1)'s phrase is otherwise a prefix of this one and the two limbs would be one ambiguous location.

figures.name: Ordinary adoption leave: weeks

tokens: ordinary adoption leave period is a period of 26 weeks

sources.citation: https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2002/2788/made (SI 2002/2788 reg 18(1) as made: "Subject to regulations 22 and 24, an employee's ordinary adoption leave period is a period of 26 weeks"; in force 8 December 2002, reg 1, and having effect only in relation to children matched with a person notified on or after 6 April 2003 or placed for adoption on or after that date, reg 3(2))
https://www.gov.uk/adoption-pay-leave (under "Leave": "Statutory Adoption Leave is 52 weeks. It's made up of: 26 weeks of Ordinary Adoption Leave 26 weeks of Additional Adoption Leave")

definitions.text: The ordinary adoption leave period: 26 weeks (regulation 18(1) of the Paternity and Adoption Leave Regulations 2002), running from the date regulation 19 fixes. The first of the two periods that make up statutory adoption leave; the second is additional adoption leave under regulation 20.
definitions.instrument: Paternity and Adoption Leave Regulations 2002 reg 18(1)

applicability.note: Attaches to the placement, not to a tax year or a pay period: regulation 19 starts the period on the date of placement or up to 14 days before it, as the employee chooses. Regulations 22 and 24 can end it early — a disrupted placement, or a dismissal. The Regulations came into force on 8 December 2002 (reg 1), but regulation 3(2) gives the adoption-leave provisions effect only for children matched with a person notified on or after 6 April 2003 or placed for adoption on or after that date, which is the date this record carries because no adoption leave period could run before it.
applicability.article: Paternity and Adoption Leave Regulations 2002 regs 1, 3(2), 18(1), 19, 22, 24

figures.scope_note: 26 weeks, and it is HALF the story: additional adoption leave adds another 26 (`employment.leave.adoption.additional_weeks`), and the 52 GOV.UK prints is their sum, published as the derived companion `employment.leave.adoption_weeks` and never as a figure any regulation states. Statutory Adoption PAY is 39 weeks and a separate figure again (`employment.sap.paid_weeks`), so the leave outruns the pay by 13 weeks. Only one member of a couple may take adoption leave; the other may qualify for paternity leave instead.
figures.notes: An SI carry (ADR-0014), and a HOST-STATES one: no textual amendment touches regulation 18(1), so the 2002 Regulations state the value by their own words and their as-made text is its own frozen witness. Both documents are hashed into this record and the verdict recomputed at Gate 2. The locator carries the whole leave-period clause because "26 weeks" alone is satisfied by three sibling provisions across this instrument and the Maternity and Parental Leave etc. Regulations 1999 — which is measured, not assumed: `locate` reports them by id.

figures.name: Statutory adoption leave: total weeks

sources.citation: https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2002/2788/made (Paternity and Adoption Leave Regulations 2002 reg 18(1): "an employee's ordinary adoption leave period is a period of 26 weeks" — the first limb of this derivation)

https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2002/2788/made (the same Regulations, reg 20(2): "an employee's additional adoption leave period is a period of 26 weeks beginning on the day after the last day of his ordinary adoption leave period" — the second limb; the Regulations state no total)

definitions.text: The whole of statutory adoption leave: the 26 weeks of ordinary adoption leave under regulation 18(1) of the Paternity and Adoption Leave Regulations 2002 plus the 26 weeks of additional adoption leave under regulation 20(2), which begins the day after the first ends. No provision states 52; it is published as a derivation from the two that do, and recomputed by the build.
definitions.instrument: Paternity and Adoption Leave Regulations 2002 reg 18(1); reg 20(2)

applicability.note: Attaches to the placement: regulation 19 starts the ordinary period on the date of placement or up to 14 days before it, and regulation 20(2) runs the additional period on from it without a gap. Dated 6 April 2003, the date regulation 3(2) gives the adoption-leave provisions effect from — the same date both limbs carry.
applicability.article: Paternity and Adoption Leave Regulations 2002 regs 3(2), 18(1), 19, 20(1), 20(2), 22, 24

figures.scope_note: 52 weeks of LEAVE, and only 39 of them carry Statutory Adoption Pay (`employment.sap.paid_weeks`), so the last 13 are unpaid unless the contract says otherwise. Regulations 22 and 24 can end the leave early — a disrupted placement, or a dismissal — so 52 is a maximum reached by an uninterrupted placement. Only one member of a couple may take it. The limbs are `employment.leave.adoption.ordinary_weeks` and `employment.leave.adoption.additional_weeks`; this record is only their sum (D14), and the build refuses a build in which the three disagree. The maternity equivalent is `employment.leave.maternity_weeks`, built the same way from the same two-limb shape.
figures.notes: Not a figure any regulation states, which is the whole reason it is a derivation: GOV.UK's adoption guide prints "Statutory Adoption Leave is 52 weeks" and is right, but right as arithmetic over two stated limbs. Both limbs are cited as legislation from the same as-made document, which is why the second receipt's citation names its regulation explicitly — the bytes behind the two are one file.

figures.name: Carer's leave: weeks per relevant period

tokens: entitled one week of carer's leave during the relevant period

sources.citation: https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2024/251/made (SI 2024/251 reg 5(1) as made: "An employee who satisfies the conditions in regulation 4 is entitled one week of carer's leave during the relevant period"; in force 6 April 2024, reg 1(2), applying to employees who give notice on or after that date, reg 2(1))

definitions.text: Carer's leave: one week of unpaid leave an employee with a dependant who has a long-term care need may take in each rolling twelve-month period (regulation 5(1) of the Carer's Leave Regulations 2024, the "relevant period" being defined by reg 5(2)). A week means the employee's own working week, measured by regulation 6.

applicability.note: Counted per relevant period — any period of twelve months running from the day the leave is taken (reg 5(2)) — not per tax year or per employer. There is no qualifying period of continuous employment: regulation 4 requires only that the employee has a dependant with a long-term care need. SI 2024/251 came into force on 6 April 2024 (reg 1(2)) and regulation 2(1) applies it to employees who give notice of an intention to take carer's leave on or after that date, so 6 April 2024 is the date this record carries on both readings.
applicability.article: Carer's Leave Regulations 2024 regs 1(2), 2(1), 4, 5(1)-(2), 6

figures.scope_note: One week, and it is the EMPLOYEE's week: regulation 6(2) gives the period they are normally required to work in a week, 6(3) divides a varying pattern's annual total by 52, and 6(4) and (5) deal with short service. The leave may be taken in individual days or half days (reg 7), so "one week" is a quantity of time and not a block. It is UNPAID — there is no carer's-pay figure to pair this with — and it is per relevant period, not per dependant.
figures.notes: An SI carry (ADR-0014), and a HOST-STATES one: no textual amendment touches regulation 5, so the 2024 Regulations state the value by their own words and their as-made text is its own frozen witness. The locator token reproduces the drafting as it stands, including the missing "to" in "is entitled one week" — read off the archived bytes, because a token that tidies the text misses. No archived GOV.UK page states the entitlement, so the record is single_source_A by design.

figures.name: Compulsory maternity leave: weeks

tokens: in respect of the period of two weeks which commences with the day on which childbirth occurs

sources.citation: https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/1999/3312/made (SI 1999/3312 reg 8 as made: "The prohibition in section 72 of the 1996 Act, against permitting an employee who satisfies prescribed conditions to work during a particular period (referred to as a 'compulsory maternity leave period'), applies- (a) in relation to an employee who is entitled to ordinary maternity leave, and (b) in respect of the period of two weeks which commences with the day on which childbirth occurs"; in force 15 December 1999, reg 1, Part II having effect only for employees whose expected week of childbirth begins on or after 30 April 2000, reg 3(1))
https://www.gov.uk/maternity-pay-leave (under "Leave": "You do not have to take 52 weeks but you must take 2 weeks' leave after your baby is born (or 4 weeks if you work in a factory)")

definitions.text: The compulsory maternity leave period: the two weeks beginning with the day childbirth occurs, during which an employer may not permit an employee entitled to ordinary maternity leave to work (regulation 8 of the Maternity and Parental Leave etc. Regulations 1999, prescribing the period for the prohibition in Employment Rights Act 1996 s.72). A prohibition on the employer, not an entitlement of the employee.
definitions.instrument: Maternity and Parental Leave etc. Regulations 1999 reg 8

applicability.note: Runs from the day of childbirth itself, so it attaches to the birth rather than to a tax year or a pay period, and no notice or qualification can shorten it. The Regulations came into force on 15 December 1999 (reg 1), but regulation 3(1) gives the provisions of Part II — which contains regulation 8 — effect "only in relation to employees whose expected week of childbirth begins on or after 30th April 2000", which is the date this record carries, because no compulsory period under this regulation could run before it.
applicability.article: Maternity and Parental Leave etc. Regulations 1999 regs 1, 3(1), 8; Employment Rights Act 1996 s.72

figures.scope_note: Two weeks, and it binds the EMPLOYER: section 72 makes permitting the work an offence, so this is the one part of maternity leave that cannot be waived. Four weeks applies instead to a woman who works in a factory, under the Public Health Act 1936 s.205 and the factories legislation GOV.UK's guide mentions — a different enactment and a separate figure, not authored. This is the stated limb GOV.UK's familiar 50 weeks of shared parental leave is computed from: 52 less these two, published as the derived maximum `employment.leave.spl.max_weeks` (D-D14-5), never as a figure any document states. Regulation 12A(5) also excludes these two weeks from the keeping-in-touch days.
figures.notes: An SI carry (ADR-0014), and a HOST-STATES one: no textual amendment touches regulation 8, so the 1999 Regulations state the value by their own words and their as-made text is its own frozen witness — which is what the 09-09 inventory could not confirm, because the as-made document was not archived until the relay parked it overnight. Both documents are hashed into this record and the verdict recomputed at Gate 2. The locator carries regulation 8(b)'s own words because "two weeks" also stands in regulation 12A(5), which cross-refers to this very period; the probe locates at `regulation-8-b`, the deepest provision that states it.

figures.name: Additional maternity leave: weeks

tokens: 26 weeks from the day on which it commenced

sources.citation: https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2002/2789/made (SI 2002/2789 reg 8(b): "In regulation 7 (duration of maternity leave periods)- ... (b) in paragraph (4), for \"29 weeks beginning with the week of childbirth\" substitute \"26 weeks from the day on which it commenced\""; in force 24 November 2002, reg 1(1), having effect only in relation to employees whose expected week of childbirth begins on or after 6 April 2003, reg 2(1))
https://www.gov.uk/maternity-pay-leave (under "Leave": "Statutory Maternity Leave is 52 weeks. It's made up of: Ordinary Maternity Leave - first 26 weeks Additional Maternity Leave - last 26 weeks")

definitions.text: The additional maternity leave period: 26 weeks from the day it commenced, which is the day after the ordinary maternity leave period ends (regulations 7(4) and 6(3) of the Maternity and Parental Leave etc. Regulations 1999). The second of the two periods that make up statutory maternity leave.
definitions.instrument: Maternity and Parental Leave etc. Regulations 1999 reg 7(4)

applicability.note: Commences the day after the last day of the ordinary maternity leave period (reg 6(3)) and runs 26 weeks from that day, so it attaches to childbirth rather than to a tax year. Regulation 7(5) ends it at a dismissal. SI 2002/2789 reg 8(b) substituted the words and came into force on 24 November 2002 (reg 1(1)), but its regulation 2(1) gives the maternity amendments effect "only in relation to employees whose expected week of childbirth begins on or after 6th April 2003" — which is the date this record carries.
applicability.article: Maternity and Parental Leave etc. Regulations 1999 regs 6(3), 7(4), 7(5); SI 2002/2789 regs 1(1), 2(1), 8(b)

figures.scope_note: READ THIS BEFORE USING THE FIGURE: 26 weeks is the SECOND half of statutory maternity leave, not the whole of it. The first half is `employment.leave.maternity.ordinary_weeks` (regulation 7(1), also 26 weeks) and the 52-week total is the derived `employment.leave.maternity_weeks`. Maternity PAY runs 39 weeks (`employment.smp.paid_leave_weeks`), so roughly the last 13 weeks of this period are unpaid; the two compulsory weeks after childbirth are `employment.leave.compulsory_maternity_weeks`.
figures.notes: An SI carry (ADR-0014): SI 2002/2789 reg 8(b) substituted the WORDS "29 weeks beginning with the week of childbirth" with "26 weeks from the day on which it commenced", and it is that substituted phrase which is the locator — verbatim in the setter's as-made text and, as it happens, unique in the host. That coincidence is exactly what its sibling lacks: reg 8(a) substituted only "26 weeks" into paragraph (1), three provisions of the host share those words, and a locator long enough to be unique there is longer than anything the setter wrote. `si_probe` uses ONE token set for the host's uniqueness test and the setter's presence test, so this row's sibling cannot be carried at all — it is authored instead as an NF-1 derivation from the same instrument's own substituted words (2026-09-14), which needs no host locator. Whether the probe should take a separate setter-side token set remains a design question, recorded rather than worked around.

figures.name: Ordinary maternity leave: weeks

sources.citation: https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2002/2789/made (SI 2002/2789 reg 8(a): "In regulation 7 (duration of maternity leave periods)- (a) in paragraph (1), for “eighteen weeks” substitute “26 weeks”"; in force 24 November 2002, reg 1(1), having effect only in relation to employees whose expected week of childbirth begins on or after 6 April 2003, reg 2(1))
https://www.gov.uk/maternity-pay-leave (under "Leave": "Statutory Maternity Leave is 52 weeks. It's made up of: Ordinary Maternity Leave - first 26 weeks Additional Maternity Leave - last 26 weeks")

https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/1999/3312/made (SI 1999/3312 reg 7(1) as made: "Subject to paragraphs (2) and (5), an employee's ordinary maternity leave period continues for the period of eighteen weeks from its commencement, or until the end of the compulsory maternity leave period provided for in regulation 8 if later"; in force 15 December 1999, reg 1, Part II — which contains regulation 7 — having effect only for employees whose expected week of childbirth begins on or after 30 April 2000, reg 3(1))

definitions.text: The ordinary maternity leave period: 26 weeks from its commencement, or until the end of the compulsory maternity leave period in regulation 8 if that is later (regulation 7(1) of the Maternity and Parental Leave etc. Regulations 1999, prescribing the period for the entitlement in Employment Rights Act 1996 s.71). The first of the two periods that make up statutory maternity leave.
definitions.instrument: Maternity and Parental Leave etc. Regulations 1999 reg 7(1)

applicability.note: Commences on the date the employee notifies under regulations 4 and 6, or earlier on the day after a pregnancy-related absence or the day after childbirth (reg 6(1)-(2)), and runs 26 weeks from that day — so it attaches to childbirth, not to a tax year or a pay period. Regulation 7(2) extends it where a statutory prohibition keeps the employee from working, and regulation 7(5) ends it at a dismissal. SI 2002/2789 reg 8(a) substituted the words and came into force on 24 November 2002 (reg 1(1)), but its regulation 2(1) gives the amendments in regulations 5 to 11 effect "only in relation to employees whose expected week of childbirth begins on or after 6th April 2003" — which is the date this record carries. The eighteen weeks before it date from 30 April 2000, the date regulation 3(1) of the 1999 Regulations gives Part II effect from, not from the 15 December 1999 commencement.
applicability.article: Maternity and Parental Leave etc. Regulations 1999 regs 3(1), 4, 6(1)-(3), 7(1), 7(2), 7(5); SI 2002/2789 regs 1(1), 2(1), 8(a); Employment Rights Act 1996 s.71

figures.scope_note: 26 weeks, and it is the FIRST half of statutory maternity leave, not the whole of it: the second half is `employment.leave.maternity.additional_weeks`, also 26 weeks, and the 52-week total is the derived `employment.leave.maternity_weeks`. Maternity PAY runs 39 weeks (`employment.smp.paid_leave_weeks`), so pay outlasts this period and stops part-way through the additional one. The first two weeks after childbirth inside it are compulsory and cannot be waived (`employment.leave.compulsory_maternity_weeks`). Regulation 7(2) can make the period longer where a statutory prohibition on working outlasts it, and regulation 7(5) ends it early on dismissal, so 26 is the ordinary length rather than an invariable one.
figures.notes: A derivation, not a carry, and deliberately so: the carry route is the one that fails here. SI 2002/2789 reg 8(a) wrote only the words "26 weeks" into paragraph (1), and `locate` reports those two words satisfied by three sibling provisions of the host (`regulation-7-1`, `regulation-7-4`, `regulation-18-1-b`), so no single token set can be both unique in the host and present in the setter — which is why this row was refused on 2026-09-11 and its sibling shipped alone. A derivation needs no host locator: it reads the amending instrument's own substituted words. What it needed was `Amendment.is_count` widened to read an integer written as a number word and followed by its unit noun, because `_COUNT`'s bare digits matched neither "eighteen weeks" nor "26 weeks" (D18 follow-up, 2026-09-14). The eighteen weeks it replaced are attested by the instrument's own for-text and dated from the 1999 Regulations' as-made bytes.

figures.name: Statutory maternity leave: total weeks

sources.citation: https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2002/2789/made (Maternity and Parental Leave (Amendment) Regulations 2002 reg 8(a), substituting "26 weeks" for "eighteen weeks" in regulation 7(1) of the Maternity and Parental Leave etc. Regulations 1999 — the ordinary maternity leave period, the first limb of this derivation)

definitions.text: The whole of statutory maternity leave: the 26 weeks of ordinary maternity leave under regulation 7(1) of the Maternity and Parental Leave etc. Regulations 1999 plus the 26 weeks of additional maternity leave under regulation 7(4), which begins the day after the first ends (reg 6(3)). No provision states 52; it is published as a derivation from the two that do, and recomputed by the build.
definitions.instrument: Maternity and Parental Leave etc. Regulations 1999 regs 7(1), 7(4)

applicability.note: Attaches to childbirth: the ordinary period commences on the date notified under regulations 4 and 6, or earlier on a pregnancy-related absence or the birth, and the additional period runs on from the day after it ends (reg 6(3)) without a gap. applicability.note: Attaches to the child: the leave may be taken only in the 52 weeks beginning with the date of birth (reg 5(2) as amended by SI 2024/329 reg 9(b), which replaced "56 days"), so neither a tax year nor a pay period governs. SI 2024/329's Parts 1 and 2 came into force on 8 March 2024 (reg 1(2)), but its regulation 5(1)(a) gives the amendments to the 2002 Regulations effect "only in respect of ... children whose expected week of birth begins after 6th April 2024". An expected week of birth begins at midnight between Saturday and Sunday, and 6 April 2024 was a Saturday, so the earliest such week begins on Sunday 7 April 2024 — which is the date this record carries, because no entitlement under the substituted paragraph can arise before it.
applicability.article: Paternity and Adoption Leave Regulations 2002 regs 4, 5(1), 5(2); SI 2024/329 regs 1(2), 5(1)(a), 9

figures.scope_note: Two weeks maximum, however many children the birth produces (twins do not double it), and the same two weeks whether taken together or as two separate single weeks. This is the BIRTH limb. Regulation 9(1) states an identical two weeks for paternity leave on an ADOPTION, and the Paternity and Adoption Leave (Adoption from Overseas) Regulations 2003 and the Paternity and Adoption Leave (Parental Orders) Regulations 2014 state it again for their own cases: separate provisions in separate instruments, none of them this record. Statutory Paternity PAY is a separate figure again (`employment.spp.weeks`, SSCBA 1992 s.171ZE(2)).
figures.notes: An SI carry (ADR-0014): SI 2024/329 reg 9(a) substituted paragraph (1) WHOLE, so there is no value-level substitution for NF-1 to re-derive and the new paragraph carries no provision id in the amender's as-made document. Note what the amendment did and did not change: the TWO WEEKS are the 2002 Regulations' own figure and have not moved, while the 2024 instrument replaced the paragraph that states them in order to allow the weeks to be split. The record is dated from that substitution because it is the text being read; the earlier period, when the same two weeks had to be taken in one continuous block, waits for a parser that can read a block substitution. The locator needs two groups: the first phrase is word-for-word identical in regulation 9(1), the adoption limb, and only "under regulation 4" separates them. THE DATE IS A CALENDAR STEP, in one sentence: SI 2024/329 reg 5(1)(a) reaches only a child whose expected week of birth begins AFTER 6 April 2024, an expected week begins at midnight between Saturday and Sunday (2002 Regulations reg 2(1)), and 6 April 2024 was a Saturday, so the first week it can reach begins on Sunday 7 April 2024. The value's own first effect under D16(d) is earlier — the 2002 Regulations fixed two weeks for children born on or after 6 April 2003 (reg 3(1)), and the 2024 instrument re-enacted the figure verbatim while splitting how it may be taken — but the probe refuses that date on these documents: at 2003-04-06 it returns MISFILED, "the setting amendment key-6c65863689c3f4f7a409f0b80e94c141 took effect 2024-03-08, after the value's stated start (2003-04-06)". A date the machinery cannot evidence is not written, so the record carries the later one and says so. D-RD-3 (D18 §1) was built for exactly this row and does NOT rescue it, because the re-enactment was not verbatim: the 2002 Regulations as made read "An employee may choose to take either one week's leave or two consecutive weeks' leave in respect of a child under regulation 4", and SI 2024/329 replaced that with "a single period of leave of either one week or two weeks, or two non-consecutive periods of leave of a week each". Same figure, different words — so the origin cannot witness the text the probe located, and the relief is refused MISFILED, "the recorded origin does not state the value". Widening the locator to a phrase common to both documents would be widening a matcher to force a match. What would settle this row is a locator the 2002 wording also carries AND that still locates uniquely in the current text — or a second value period, once a parser can read a block substitution.

definitions.instrument: Maternity and Parental Leave etc. Regulations 1999 reg 10(1C)

applicability.note: Measured from a birth event, not from a tax year, a pay period or the redundancy: the 18 months begin with the first day of the expected week of childbirth unless the employer has been notified of the actual day of childbirth before the end of the maternity leave period, in which case they begin with that day (reg 10(1C)(b), (1D)). definitions.text: HMRC's advisory fuel rates: the amount per business mile, by fuel type and engine size (by charging location for a fully electric car), at or below which an employer may reimburse an employee for fuel used on business travel in a COMPANY car — or at or above which an employee must repay the cost of fuel used for private travel — without a taxable profit arising and without Class 1A National Insurance being due. The rates are ADVISORY and non-statutory: no Act or instrument states them. The Income Tax (Earnings and Pensions) Act 2003 charges the car fuel benefit and treats excess reimbursement as earnings without fixing any rate per mile, and HMRC publishes these figures as the cost per mile it will accept; an employer may use a higher rate where it can show the actual fuel cost per mile is higher, and its own lower rate where its cars are more efficient. The key is (fuel, band): the engine-size band HMRC prints for petrol, diesel and LPG, and the charging location for electric.

applicability.note: Fixed by the date of the business journey being reimbursed (or of the private travel being repaid): the table in force on that date applies, and HMRC's guidance allows the previous quarter's rates to be used for up to one month from the date new rates apply. There is no statutory provision; the governing text is the guidance page itself, "When you can use the mileage rates".
applicability.article: HMRC guidance "Advisory fuel rates", "When you can use the mileage rates" ("You can use the previous rates for up to 1 month from the date any new rates apply"); no statutory provision

figures.scope_note: ADVISORY, NON-STATUTORY. HMRC reviews the rates quarterly on 1 March, 1 June, 1 September and 1 December and dates each table itself; the previous rates may be used for up to one month from the date new rates apply. Company cars only: an employee's own vehicle takes the statutory approved mileage allowance payments (employment.mileage.amap.*), which are a different figure. Hybrid cars are treated as petrol or diesel. The diesel bands split at 1600cc where petrol and LPG split at 1400cc, which is why the key is (fuel, band) rather than one engine-size axis. HMRC has published separate home-charging and public-charging electric rates since 1 September 2025; the earlier quarterly tables the page still prints (2024-09-01 to 2024-11-30; 2024-12-01 to 2025-02-28; 2025-03-01 to 2025-05-31; 2025-06-01 to 2025-08-31) carry one undivided electric rate, a different key domain, and are not carried by this record — rates from an earlier date are on the National Archives timeline the page links to. Electricity is not a fuel for car fuel benefit purposes; the electric rate is the advisory electric rate HMRC publishes beside the fuel rates.
figures.notes: An administrative table (D23(c)): HMRC is the administering authority and its own guidance page is the A-document, hashed in the receipt and re-read by this script, which parses every dated table on the page and refuses to write a quarter whose cells or dates differ from what was authored. Each value is dated exactly as the page dates its table ("From 1 September 2026", "From 1 June 2026 to 31 August 2026", ...), the closed quarters with the end date the page states and `superseded` as their terminal kind. A value's `enacted_date` is the day HMRC published that quarter's table, read from the page's own change history ("The advisory fuel rates from 1 September 2026 have been added", 2026-08-21) — the made date of a table that has no instrument, and what lets a quarter HMRC publishes ahead of its start classify as enacted rather than announced; a quarter no note names carries none, and where HMRC corrected a cell before the quarter began the correction's date is the one carried, because that is the table the page now prints (the public charger rate from 1 September 2025, "has been updated", 2025-08-26). The employers' rates-and-thresholds page, as archived, prints the quarter from 2026-06-01 ("These rates apply from …"), so that value is corroborated by two official pages and every other quarter is single-source A: the page states them or it does not, and a guidance receipt for a page that does not print the table would freeze the value's freshness on a page that says nothing about it. Rate cells are held as money (£0.14) because that is what every other money figure is and what the API projects; the pence spelling is a matching form (source_match.value_forms), as for the AMAP passenger rate.

definitions.text: HMRC's National Insurance category letters and what each one selects. For every letter HMRC prints: the employer-side relief the letter operates — `standard` (the secondary threshold and the secondary percentage); `under_21`, `apprentice_under_25` and `veteran` (a nil secondary rate up to the upper secondary threshold of that name); `freeport` and `investment_zone` (a nil secondary rate up to the special-tax-site upper secondary threshold); `no_liability` — and the employee-side class — `standard` (the main and additional primary percentages above the primary threshold); `married_women_reduced` (the reduced rate under a certificate of election); `deferred` (the additional-rate percentage only, the main rate being paid in another employment); `over_state_pension_age` (no primary contribution); `no_liability` — together with the employee group HMRC prints beside the letter. The letters are HMRC's payroll codes: no Act or instrument prints them. This record holds no threshold and no rate; those stay in the records that own them (employment.ni.class1.*), which a letter's codes select.
definitions.instrument: HMRC guidance, "National Insurance rates and categories" — "Category letters" (www.gov.uk/national-insurance-rates-letters); no statutory instrument prints the letters

applicability.note: The letter an employer operates for an earnings period selects the secondary threshold and the employee rate class applied to that period's earnings. The letter itself has no statutory force; its legal effect is that of the provisions behind the records the codes select — Social Security Contributions and Benefits Act 1992 ss. 6, 8 and 9 (Class 1 liability and the primary and secondary percentages), s. 9A (the age-related secondary percentage, under 21s) and s. 9B (zero-rate secondary contributions for apprentices), and the National Insurance Contributions Act 2022 (freeport and investment-zone tax sites, veterans), whose thresholds are those records' values.
applicability.article: Social Security Contributions and Benefits Act 1992 ss. 6, 8, 9, 9A, 9B; National Insurance Contributions Act 2022 s. 8 (the upper secondary thresholds the reliefs run to); the letter is HMRC's code, not a provision

figures.scope_note: A LOOKUP, not a table of numbers: each letter resolves to two codes, and the thresholds and percentages a code names are the existing records (employment.ni.class1.secondary_threshold, .ust, .aust, .veterans_ust, .freeport_ust, .primary_threshold, .employee_main_rate, .employee_additional_rate, .married_women_reduced_rate, .employer_secondary_rate); a second copy of a threshold here would be the drift ADR-0013 §3 forbids. The codes are read from HMRC's own "Employee group" description of each letter and checked against the shape of the contribution tables on both pages (letters sharing a code share a rate row). Letter X (no liability, for example under 16s) is stated in prose on HMRC's page and on no rates table. HMRC's page dates its tables for the tax year 6 April 2026 to 5 April 2027 and states no earlier date for the letters; the Freeport letters (2022), the Investment Zone letters (2024) and V (2021) predate it, so this value says which letters are in use from 6 April 2026 and nothing about when each was introduced. No `figure_ref` output yet: a figure_ref must resolve on every entry, and neither an investment-zone upper secondary threshold (refused 2026-09-14, NICA 2022 s. 8 as archived names no investment zone) nor any threshold for X exists to point at. Employees who could carry more than one letter take the one HMRC's guidance directs, which this record does not decide.
figures.notes: An administrative table (D23(c)): HMRC is the administering authority and its own guidance page is the A-document, hashed in the receipt and re-read by this script. Every letter is read from the page's "Category letter / Employee group" tables (X from its paragraph) and refused if the page's set differs from the script's; each code is refused unless the words it is read from are in that letter's description ("under 21", "Apprentices under 25", "(veterans)", "special tax site within a Freeport", "... within an Investment Zone", "Married women and widows" with "reduced National Insurance", "defer National Insurance", "State Pension age", "do not have to pay National Insurance"), `standard` being the absence of every other code's words on that side. The employers' rates-and-thresholds page is the B side: it prints the same sixteen rated letters with HMRC's own bracketed glosses, each checked against the codes, so the value is corroborated; X is on no second page. The value is dated from the sentence the page dates its tables with, and the script refuses when that sentence goes.

definitions.text: The "appropriate amount" Employment Rights Act 1996 s.162(2)(b) allows for each year of employment in which the employee was not below the age of 22 but was below 41, in the statutory redundancy payment calculation: one week's pay for a year of employment (not within paragraph (a)) in which he was not below the age of twenty-two. A MULTIPLIER on a week's pay, applied once per reckonable year, and not a sum of money.

applicability.note: Applied year by year in the calculation s.162(1) directs: the period of continuous employment ending with the relevant date is reckoned BACKWARDS from its end and the appropriate amount is allowed for each year within it (s.162(1)(a)-(c)). The age is the employee's age in the year of employment being counted, so a single dismissal can draw on all three multipliers. Section 162(3) stops the reckoning at twenty years (`employment.redundancy.service_cap_years`): where twenty years have been reckoned, no account is taken of any year earlier than those twenty, so what the cap discards is the service furthest from the relevant date.
applicability.article: Employment Rights Act 1996 s.162(1)-(3); s.227; s.234

figures.scope_note: ONE limb of three, published separately because the statute states them separately: s.162(2) defines "the appropriate amount" in three lettered paragraphs and this record is paragraph (b) alone. The other two are `employment.redundancy.age_multiplier.under_22` and `employment.redundancy.age_multiplier.41_and_over`. The week's pay each multiplier is applied to is the one Employment Rights Act 1996 s.234 defines and s.227 caps (`employment.redundancy.weekly_pay_cap`), so the money a year of employment is worth moves every April while these numbers do not. Subsections (4), (5) and (8) — the taper that cut the payment by a twelfth for each month after the employee's 64th birthday — were REPEALED on 1 October 2006 by the Employment Equality (Age) Regulations 2006 (S.I. 2006/1031), so no age ceiling survives; the age FLOORS in subsection (2) itself were not touched and are the bands these three records carry.
figures.notes: An act carry (N1): s.162(2)(b) states the multiplier in WORDS — "one week's pay" — and no substring matcher derives a form of the number from them, so the locator is a hand-authored LOCATORS phrase read from the paragraph itself; the GOV.UK sentence is registered in B_EVIDENCE for the nightly. The token carries the paragraph's whole limb because the three are told apart by their AGE clause and not by the multiplier. FOUR F-notes stand on s.162 — "S. 162(4)(5)(8) repealed (1.10.2006)", "S. 162(7) repealed (15.12.1999)" and two separate substitutions of words in s. 162(6), on 1.8.1998 and 1.10.2006 — and NONE touches subsection (2), so the probe reaches ACT-HOLDS on the subsection's own untouched words without needing D-RD-1's touched-other-words relief; the ten C-notes recorded on the block modify Part 11's application, not its text. It is the amount an individual may elect to transfer under s.55C — the amount by which the transferor's own personal allowance is reduced (s.55B(6)), and the amount on which the recipient's tax reduction is calculated. The Act states the rule and no figure, so the number is published as a derivation from the personal allowance and recomputed by the build.

definitions.text: The proportion of the excess by which the personal allowance is withdrawn: for an individual whose adjusted net income exceeds the income limit, the allowance is reduced by one-half of the excess (Income Tax Act 2007 s.35(2)). The value is that fraction — 0.5 OF THE EXCESS, not 50% of the allowance and not a rate of tax — so 50 pence of allowance is lost for every £1 of income above the limit, which is the £1-for-every-£2 rule GOV.UK states in money.

applicability.note: Assessed on the tax year's adjusted net income; PAYE reflects it through the tax code. The reduction runs until the allowance reaches nil and no further — s.35(2) reduces "the allowance under subsection (1)", so the withdrawal stops at zero — and s.35(3) rounds what remains UP to the nearest whole pound.

figures.scope_note: Unchanged since 6 April 2010, and the OTHER half of a pair: the income limit this fraction applies above is `employment.tax.pa_taper_threshold` (£100,000) and the allowance it withdraws is `employment.tax.personal_allowance`. The £125,140 at which the allowance reaches nil is arithmetic on all three and is not published as a figure of its own. Read the value as a multiplier on the EXCESS: a £110,000 income is £10,000 over the limit, so £5,000 of allowance goes. The effective marginal rate of 60% that commentators quote is the consequence of this fraction meeting the 40% band, not something any provision states.
figures.notes: An act carry whose touching note carries no date of its own — "with effect in accordance with s. 4(4) of the amending Act" — and the same note that inserted s.35(2) whole, so this row and `employment.tax.pa_taper_threshold` resolve through one document and share a date. The value is a `ratio` because the statute states a FRACTION: 0.5 is one-half of the excess, and a `percentage` would publish a "50%" the section does not contain and invite the reader to apply it to the allowance. No form of 0.5 appears in the section either — `components()` returns None for a float as it does for a bare int — so the locator is a hand-authored LOCATORS phrase read from subsection (2) itself, and the GOV.UK sentence is registered in B_EVIDENCE so the nightly re-checks the B side. The B page states the rule in money ("£1 for every £2") and never the fraction: it corroborates the RULE, which is what this record holds.

So the 1998 Regulations state the value by their own words and their as-made text is its own frozen witness. The archived drafting is "is an uninterrupted period", not "shall be": the token is read off the bytes, not modernised. No archived GOV.UK page states the 20 minutes, so the record is single_source_A by design.

definitions.text: The minimum daily rest a worker is entitled to: not less than eleven consecutive hours in each 24-hour period worked (regulation 10(1) of the Working Time Regulations 1998). Rest BETWEEN working days, not a break within one.

applicability.note: Measured over each 24-hour period during which the worker works for the employer, not over a pay period or a tax year. applicability.article: Working Time Regulations 1998 regs 1(1), 10(1); SI 2002/3128 reg 11

figures.scope_note: Eleven consecutive hours in every 24, and CONSECUTIVE is the word that matters: two separate blocks do not satisfy it. A young worker gets twelve under regulation 10(2), a separate figure (`employment.working_time.young_worker.rest_period_daily_hours`), and regulation 10(3) lets a young worker's period be interrupted where an adult's may not. figures.notes: An SI carry (ADR-0014), and a HOST-STATES one under D18 §2: SI 2002/3128 reg 11 substituted "An adult worker" with "A worker", and its located span prints no part of the eleven hours, so the amendment touched other words of the provision and not the value. figures.name: Weekly rest period: uninterrupted hours

tokens: uninterrupted rest period of not less than 24 hours in each seven-day period

sources.citation: https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/1998/1833/made (SI 1998/1833 reg 11(1) as made: "Subject to paragraph (2), an adult worker is entitled to an uninterrupted rest period of not less than 24 hours in each seven-day period during which he works for his employer"; in force 1 October 1998, reg 1(1))

definitions.text: The minimum weekly rest a worker is entitled to: an uninterrupted period of not less than 24 hours in each seven-day period worked (regulation 11(1) of the Working Time Regulations 1998). Regulation 11(4) fixes when the seven-day period begins.

applicability.note: Measured over each seven-day period during which the worker works for the employer; regulation 11(4) begins that period where a relevant agreement provides or, failing that, at the start of each week. applicability.article: Working Time Regulations 1998 regs 1(1), 11(1), 11(2), 11(4); SI 2002/3128 reg 12

figures.scope_note: 24 uninterrupted hours a week, and paragraph (1) is "subject to paragraph (2)": if the employer so determines, the worker takes either two such periods in a 14-day period or one uninterrupted 48 hours in the same 14 days instead — an alternative to this entitlement, not an addition to it, and neither figure is this record. A young worker's 48 hours in every SEVEN days is a different provision again (reg 11(3), `employment.working_time.young_worker.rest_period_weekly_hours`), and regulation 11(7) says the weekly rest does not include any part of a daily rest period except where that is justified.
figures.notes: An SI carry (ADR-0014), and a HOST-STATES one under D18 §2: SI 2002/3128 reg 12 substituted "an adult worker" with "a worker" in paragraphs (1), (2) and (7), and its located span prints no part of the 24 hours, so the amendment touched other words of the provision and not the value. figures.name: Annual leave: statutory minimum (weeks)

sources.citation: https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2001/3256/made (Working Time Regulations 1998 reg 13(1), as substituted by SI 2001/3256 reg 2(2): "a worker is entitled to four weeks' annual leave in each leave year" — the first limb of this derivation; the 1998 Regulations state no total)

https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2007/2079/made (SI 2007/2079 reg 2(2), inserting reg 13A into the 1998 Regulations, whose paragraph (2)(e) reads "in any leave year beginning on or after 1st April 2009, 1.6 weeks" — the second limb; the instrument's explanatory note describes the effect as an increase "from 4 weeks to 5.6 weeks", but no regulation says 5.6)

definitions.text: The statutory minimum paid annual leave a worker is entitled to in a leave year: the four weeks of regulation 13(1) of the Working Time Regulations 1998 plus the 1.6 weeks of regulation 13A(2)(e). No provision states 5.6; it is published as a derivation from the two figures that do, and recomputed by the build.

applicability.note: Counted per leave year, and the leave year is the worker's own: regulation 13(3) fixes it by a relevant agreement or by the anniversary of the date the employment began, and regulation 13A(4) gives regulation 13A the same one. Dated from the later limb, 1 April 2009: before the first leave year beginning on that date the additional pot was one of regulation 13A(2)(a) to (d)'s smaller transitional amounts, so the sum was not 5.6.
applicability.article: Working Time Regulations 1998 regs 13(1), 13(3), 13A(2)(e), 13A(3), 13A(4), 15B

figures.scope_note: 5.6 weeks is a minimum in WEEKS, and regulation 13A(3) caps the same aggregate at 28 DAYS — so a worker on a six-day week accrues 33.6 days under this figure and receives 28 (`employment.working_time.annual_leave_days_cap`). The two limbs are `employment.working_time.annual_leave_weeks` and `employment.working_time.additional_annual_leave_weeks`; this record is only their sum (D14), and the build refuses a build in which the three disagree. It does NOT apply to an irregular-hours or part-year worker in a leave year beginning on or after 1 April 2024: they accrue hours under regulation 15B at 12.07% instead (`employment.working_time.irregular_hours_accrual_pct`), which is a different entitlement and not a different spelling of this one. The two pots are also paid differently — the four weeks at the "normal" rate and the 1.6 at the "basic" rate — which is why the limbs are the records and this is the companion.
figures.notes: Not a figure any regulation states, which is the whole reason it is a derivation: SI 2007/2079's explanatory note describes the effect as an increase "from 4 weeks to 5.6 weeks", and an explanatory note is not the enacting text. GOV.UK states 5.6 weeks on the holiday guide, and it is right — but it is right as arithmetic, so the corpus publishes the arithmetic and recomputes it rather than quoting the total and letting it rot. Both limbs are cited as legislation. This is the second scalar `ratio` in the corpus, after the 1.6-week limb it reads.

figures.name: Young worker: maximum daily working time

definitions.text: The limit on a young worker's working time in a day: eight hours (regulation 5A(1)(a) of the Working Time Regulations 1998). A hard limit on the day itself, not an average over a reference period, and hours worked for more than one employer are aggregated (reg 5A(2)).

applicability.note: Applies to each DAY worked, aggregating the hours worked for every employer (reg 5A(2)); there is no reference period and no averaging. A "young worker" is a worker over compulsory school age and under 18 (reg 2(1)). SI 2002/3128 inserted regulation 5A and came into force on 6 April 2003 by its own regulation 1 ("shall come into force on 6th April 2003"), which is the date this record carries.
applicability.article: Working Time Regulations 1998 regs 5A(1)(a), 5A(2), 5A(4); reg 2(1) for "young worker"; SI 2002/3128 reg 1

figures.scope_note: Eight hours a day for a young worker, and there is NO individual opt-out — unlike the adult's 48-hour week, which regulation 5 lets a worker agree out of. Regulation 27A(1) disapplies regulation 5A where the work is needed to maintain continuity of service or production or to meet a surge in demand, no adult worker is available and the young worker's education would not suffer. The weekly limb is `employment.working_time.young_worker.max_weekly_hours`; a young worker's night work is prohibited outright by regulation 6A rather than limited.
figures.notes: An SI carry (ADR-0014): SI 2002/3128 reg 6 INSERTED regulation 5A whole, so there is no value-level substitution for NF-1 to re-derive and the inserted text carries no provision ids in the amender's own document. The evidence is the pair: the 1998 Regulations' current view and SI 2002/3128 as made, both hashed and recomputed at Gate 2. Nothing preceded this value: before 6 April 2003 the Regulations set no limit on a young worker's hours at all. The locator token is "eight hours a day" and not the host's run-together serialisation of paragraph (1), because a token has to satisfy the setter's document too.

definitions.text: The limit on a young worker's working time in a week: 40 hours (regulation 5A(1)(b) of the Working Time Regulations 1998), the week starting at midnight between Sunday and Monday (reg 5A(3)).
